title: Homo erectus
wiki_lead:
Homo erectus ( lit. 'upright man') is an extinct species of archaic human from the Pleistocene, spanning nearly 2 million years. It is the first human species to evolve a humanlike body plan and gait, to leave Africa and colonize Asia and Europe, and to wield fire. Some populations of H. erectus were ancestors of later human species, including H. heidelbergensis—the last common ancestor of modern humans, Neanderthals, and Denisovans. As such a widely distributed species both geographically and temporally, H. erectus anatomy varies considerably. Subspecies are sometimes recognized: H. e. erectus, H. e. pekinensis, H. e. soloensis, H. e. ergaster, H. e. georgicus, and H. e. tautavelensis.
The species was first described by Eugène Dubois in 1893 as "Pithecanthropus erectus" using a skullcap, molar, and femur from Java, Indonesia. Further discoveries around East Asia were used to contend that humanity evolved out of Asia. Based on historical race concepts, it was argued that local H. erectus populations evolved directly into local modern human populations (polycentrism) rather than all humanity sharing a single anatomically modern ancestor (monogenism). As the fossil record improved over the mid-to-late 20th century, the "Out of Africa" theory and monogenism became the consensus.
The typical skull has a pronounced brow ridge, a protruding jaw, and large teeth. The bones are much thicker than in modern humans. East Asian populations normally have an even more robust skeleton and larger brain volume—averaging 1,000 cc (61 cu in). Western H. erectus brain volume could be as low as 546 cc (33.3 cu in) in H. e. georgicus. H. erectus probably had a faster apelike growth trajectory, lacking the extended childhood required for language acquisition. Reconstructed adult body dimensions range from 141–167 cm (4 ft 8 in – 5 ft 6 in) in height and about 50 kg (110 lb) in weight.
H. erectus invented the Acheulean tool industry, a major innovation of large, heavy-duty stone tools. These may have been used in butchery, vegetable processing, and woodworking of spears and digging sticks. H. erectus was a major predator of large herbivores on the expanding savannas during the Quaternary glaciation. The species is usually characterized as the first hunter-gatherer and the first to practice sexual division of labor. Fire usage and cave habitation were probably not important aspects of daily life. Similarly, H. erectus may not have often ventured into colder regions or cooked meat. The last known occurrence of H. erectus is 108,000 to 117,000 years ago (H. e. soloensis) in Southeast Asia, until the last savannas in the region gave way to jungle.

Research history

While Charles Darwin had hypothesized in his 1871 Descent of Man that humans most likely evolved in Africa, many late-19th century evolutionary naturalists postulated that Asia  was the birthplace of humankind. Asia is midway between all continents via land routes or short sea crossings, providing optimal dispersal routes throughout the world. Among the major proponents of "Out of Asia" theory was Ernst Haeckel, who argued that the first human species (which he speculatively named Homo primigenius) evolved on a now-disproven hypothetical continent "Lemuria" from a species he termed Pithecanthropus alalus (speechless ape-man). "Lemuria" had supposedly sunk below the Indian Ocean, accounting for the lack of fossil evidence.
Dutch scientist Eugène Dubois joined the Royal Netherlands East Indies Army to search for the "missing link" of human evolution in Java. At the Trinil site, his team found a skullcap and molar in 1891, and a femur in 1892 (Java Man), which he named "Pithecanthropus erectus" in 1893. He attempted to convince the European scientific community that he had found an upright-walking ape-man dating to the late Pliocene or Early Pleistocene; they dismissed his findings as some kind of non-human ape.

grok_lead: Homo erectus is an extinct species of archaic human in the genus Homo, known for being the first hominin to migrate out of Africa and exhibit modern-like body proportions, with a temporal range spanning approximately 2 million to 108,000 years ago. Fossils indicate that early H. erectus originated in Africa around 1.9 million years ago, with populations later dispersing across Eurasia, including sites in Georgia, China, Indonesia, and recent evidence from Spain suggesting presence in Western Europe. This species is distinguished by its robust physical build, including a low forehead, prominent supraorbital torus (brow ridge), and thick cranial bones, alongside a body height that could reach up to 1.85 meters in adulthood, as evidenced by the nearly complete skeleton of the Nariokotome Boy (KNM-WT 15000) from Kenya dated to about 1.5 million years ago. Physically, H. erectus displayed a mix of primitive and derived traits, with an average brain size increasing over time from around 600â800 cmÂ³ in early specimens to over 1,000 cmÂ³ in later ones, representing about 60â75% of modern human cranial capacity. Their postcranial skeleton was adapted for efficient bipedal locomotion, with long legs and narrow pelvises similar to those of Homo sapiens, enabling endurance walking and running across diverse environments from savannas to high-altitude steppes. Dentition featured large molars with robust roots but reduced canine size compared to earlier hominins, suggesting a diet that included tough plant material, meat from scavenging or hunting, and possibly cooked food. Key fossils, such as the Dmanisi skulls from Georgia (dated to 1.8 million years ago), reveal variability in stature and brain size, with some individuals as short as modern humans but with smaller brains around 600 cmÂ³. Culturally, H. erectus is notable for technological innovations, including the development of Acheulean stone toolsâsuch as symmetrical hand axesâby around 1.75 million years ago, which surpassed the simpler Oldowan tools of earlier hominins. Evidence from sites like Melka Kunture in Ethiopia shows that H. erectus produced both Oldowan and early Acheulean tools as early as 2 million years ago, indicating behavioral flexibility in high-altitude settings over 2,000 meters. The species is also associated with the controlled use of fire, with potential evidence from burned bones and hearths dating back to 780,000 years ago in Israel, though earlier claims around 1.9 million years ago remain debated. These adaptations supported their wide dispersal and long-term survival in varied climates, from tropical Asia to temperate Eurasia. The evolutionary role of H. erectus is significant, as it may represent the direct ancestor to later species like Homo heidelbergensis and possibly Homo sapiens, with some evidence suggesting interbreeding based on shared dental and skeletal traits identified in recent studies. African populations, sometimes classified separately as Homo ergaster, show more advanced traits and are seen as the stem from which non-African H. erectus derived. Iconic discoveries include Java Man (Trinil 2, ~700,000â1,000,000 years ago) and Peking Man (Zhoukoudian, 700,000â400,000 years ago), which highlight the species' persistence in Southeast Asia until its eventual extinction, potentially outlasted by incoming Homo sapiens.
